narrative: Today's batch leans heavily on fire and post-disturbance ecology: a six-month camera-trap study in Namibian savanna finds mammal occupancy declining progressively in burned areas while small carnivores and burrow-associated species suffer the steepest losses, and adjacent 'proximal' zones fail to act as refugia. In movement and behaviour, a habitat-selection review argues that ignoring fitness and health proxies risks protecting ecological sink habitats, while a free-ranging lizard study shows UV exposure is actively regulated as a physiological axis distinct from thermoregulation. Climate-driven vulnerability work spans amphibian biogeography (identifying long-term climate refugia for torrent frogs) and fish metabolic scaling, both pointing to size- and range-dependent exposure to warming. A landscape ecology paper questions whether regenerating forestry clearcuts function as ecological traps for caribou by concentrating predation risk, and a nutritional-ecology study of Acacia gazelles shows diet and secondary-metabolite avoidance shaping reintroduction planning. Invasion ecology contributes a plant-pollinator 'invasional meltdown' example, where an introduced tree facilitates the spread of an introduced bee. On the methods side, several Methods in Ecology and Evolution papers push bioacoustic and eDNA toolkits forward, including a novel-class-identification task for passive acoustic monitoring and a new evolutionary algorithm for real-time bioacoustic classification.
